extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism students, newsroom editors, and engaged citizens
extracted.subtask_description: Normative standards and evaluative criteria for what journalism should do and how journalists should work — the core principles (the 'elements of journalism') that define good, democratic journalism and guidance on applying them across changing technologies and business pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of journalism is to provide people with the information they need to be free and self-governing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching normative aim that justifies journalistic practices and shapes other elements; journalism should produce independent, reliable, accurate, and comprehensive information that citizens require to take part in governing themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism's first obligation is to the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism's first obligation is to the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is the primary duty; reporting must aim for accuracy and factual correctness. This ties directly to verification practices and resisting distortion, deception, or rushed inaccuracies driven by other incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Its first loyalty is to citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Its first loyalty is to citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' primary allegiance should be to the public, not to advertisers, owners, political actors, or other special interests. Editorial decisions should be guided by citizens' needs rather than corporate or commercial priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essence is a discipline of verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Its essence is a discipline of verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification — systematic checking, sourcing, and corroboration — is the core technique that distinguishes journalism from other forms of communication (rumor, propaganda, advertising). The book emphasizes learning and practicing verification routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independence from those covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Its practitioners must maintain an independence from those they cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence requires resisting influence from subjects, advertisers, owners, and political powers. The text notes that independence is often conflated with neutrality and warns that true independence does not mean unthinking neutrality; it means avoiding conflicts of interest and undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve as an independent monitor of power
rubrics_metrics.description: It must serve as an independent monitor of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism should expose misuse of power, hold leaders accountable, and investigate institutions. The book gives examples of government-produced media, deceptive VNRs, paid content and other forms of manipulation to illustrate threats to the watchdog role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a forum for public criticism and compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: It must provide a forum for public criticism and compromise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News outlets should create spaces where public issues are aired, debated, and where collective problem-solving and compromise can emerge. This includes coverage that surfaces differing perspectives and facilitates civic conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the significant interesting and relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: It must strive to make the significant interesting and relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism should tell important stories in compelling ways so people will pay attention — combining substantive importance with engaging presentation rather than pandering to triviality or mere entertainment value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the news comprehensive and in proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: It must keep the news comprehensive and in proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should reflect the relative importance of events and issues, avoid disproportionate emphasis on sensational items, and strive for breadth so the public gets a full, contextual picture of the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to exercise personal conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Its practitioners have an obligation to exercise their personal conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must apply individual ethical judgment; professional norms do not absolve personal responsibility. This covers decisions about exposing wrongdoing, resisting improper directives, and acting on moral judgment even under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizens' rights and responsibilities regarding news
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens, too, have rights and responsibilities when it comes to the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A healthy journalism ecosystem requires citizens who demand independent information, engage critically, and use news to participate in self-governance. The public must understand and expect the principles of journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: News satisfies the Awareness Instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: News satisfies a basic human 'Awareness Instinct' — an intrinsic need to know what is occurring beyond direct experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This psychological underpinning explains why people seek news and why certain story types recur cross-culturally. Recognizing this helps journalists choose stories that meet the public's need for awareness, security, and social bonding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities expected of news gatherers/messengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Messengers should be able to 'run swiftly over the next hill, accurately gather information, and engagingly retell it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical criteria for reporters: speed in newsgathering, factual accuracy in collection and reporting, and the ability to present information in an engaging, comprehensible form. These skills together constitute good reporting practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide independent, reliable, accurate, and comprehensive information
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism provides something unique: independent, reliable, accurate, and comprehensive information that citizens require to be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrasing summarizes the qualities journalism must deliver to serve democracy; it is both a goal and an evaluative standard for news organizations' output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against commercialization and entertainment substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid journalism being subsumed by business pressures, turning news into entertainment or corporate promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights problems such as bonuses tied to profits, conglomerate owners using news for corporate advantage, and news prioritized for entertainment metrics. Journalists and organizations should resist incentives that prioritize revenue over public-interest reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence does not equal neutrality; beware of objectivity myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence is not the same as neutrality; the concept of objectivity has been 'mangled' and is often misused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book warns against treating neutrality as an end in itself; instead accountability, verification, and fairness should guide coverage. Objectivity should be understood as a method (verification, transparency about methods), not false balance or neutrality for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize principles over techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between the principles that guide journalism's purpose and the techniques one generation develops in a specific medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles (truth, independence, verification, public service) should remain constant even as techniques (radio, TV, internet) change; adapt methods while preserving core values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery through repetition and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution to journalism's problems lies in producers mastering the principles and rigorously applying them through repeated practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical change is achieved not by single dramatic reforms but by continual practice until principles become second nature — training, routines, and newsroom culture are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to government-produced media and paid/placed content
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and resist government-produced media, deceptive video news releases, paid columnists, and other forms of covert propaganda or paid content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents examples (deceptive VNRs, paid placement in foreign/local media, paid U.S. columnists) and implies journalists should identify, disclose, and refuse to pass off such materials as independent news.
